html:
Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar was an astrophysicist, born in 1910 in Lahore to a Tamil family, who worked out how stars die. He won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1983. His uncle C. V. Raman, his father's younger brother, had won it in 1930.

He grew up in Madras and studied physics at Presidency College there. In 1930, aged 19, he sailed for Trinity College at Cambridge. On the voyage he put relativity together with the new quantum physics and found a limit. A dying star heavier than about 1.4 times the Sun cannot settle down as a white dwarf. It must go on collapsing. This is the Chandrasekhar limit, and it points to neutron stars and black holes.

In 1935 Arthur Eddington, the leading astronomer in Britain, mocked the idea at a public meeting. For years few astronomers took his side. He turned out to be right.

In 1937 he joined the University of Chicago and its Yerkes Observatory, and he stayed for the rest of his life. He became a US citizen in 1953 and died in Chicago in 1995. He wrote standard books on the structure of stars, the movement of stars in galaxies, the passage of light through gas, the stability of fluids and the mathematics of black holes. He edited the Astrophysical Journal from 1952 to 1971.

During the Second World War he worked on shock waves and the flight of shells for the US Army at Aberdeen in Maryland. His skill in the physics of fluids led Robert Oppenheimer to invite him to join the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos. His security clearance came through too slowly, and he never worked on the bomb. A rumour, never confirmed, says he visited the project's calutrons, the machines that separated uranium.

NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory, launched in 1999, is named after him.
